parsed.response: STRENGTHS: (1) Clear, validated pain point: a 412-respondent survey shows 61% bought formalwear never worn again, avg 1.4 wears per piece, and informal group-chat borrowing already exists as revealed demand. (2) Real traction for a student pilot: 187 accounts, 241 listings, 63 paid renters in six weeks, 44% repeat rental within the window, strong supply-side liquidity (more items listed than users renting). (3) Sensible, simple unit economics at the surface: 70% borrower savings, lender earns money on idle assets, 15% borrower fee plus 10% resale fee plus damage waiver. (4) Credible founder-market fit and complementary team (ops with direct sorority closet experience, engineer who built the app, growth/design), 8 months working together. (5) Focused wedge with hyperlocal density, event-based search and verified .edu accounts; seasonal demand is predictable. (6) Capital-efficient ask with a reasonable allocation tied to the product gaps (payments, protection, verification) and legal formation. WEAKNESSES: (1) Very small absolute economics: 1,940 dollars GMV and about 291 dollars fee revenue in the pilot; 12-month forecast of about 9,000 dollars revenue is tiny and does not yet suggest a venture-scale business. Break-even claim is 'direct costs' only. (2) Market sizing is top-down and inflated: 2-3B 'addressable' is total formalwear spend, not rental-addressable revenue; the 50M+ transaction volume at 5% share conflicts with the stated 6M-student serviceable base and 3-4 events/year assumptions, and rental prices are far below purchase prices, so revenue per student would be far smaller than spend. Realistic revenue per user (4.65 dollars per rental, 3-4 rentals/year) is roughly 15-20 dollars per user per year, which caps campus-level revenue and makes unit economics thin. (3) Core mechanics are not yet built: in-app payments, deposits, damage protection and verified onboarding are funded by the ask, so the pilot likely ran on informal payment, meaning leakage, trust and disintermediation risks are untested. (4) Pilot evidence is single-campus and short; only 34% of accounts rented (63/187), 44% repeat is within six weeks of a small cohort, and there is no evidence of cross-campus repeatability or retention across seasons. (5) Heavy seasonality and low frequency (a few events per year) limit engagement and lifetime value; 'low CAC' is asserted, not measured. (6) Disintermediation and leakage risk: once two students meet in person, they can transact off-platform; 15% fee is vulnerable. (7) Operational and liability issues are underdeveloped: damage, loss, cleaning, sizing disputes, insurance, fraud, and trust and safety on a two-sided marketplace; deposit disputes can sour small student communities. (8) Competitive defensibility is modest: campus density is hard to build campus by campus and replicable by Facebook groups, Poshmark/Depop-style apps, or Rent the Runway adding student programs; graduating-class churn constantly erodes the user base. (9) Execution constraints: founders are full-time students (seniors who graduate), no legal entity yet, only 2,400 dollars self-funded, and expansion from one to five campuses with a three-person team requires ambassadors and local ops that are costly relative to per-campus revenue. OVERALL: Strong problem validation, enthusiastic early traction and sensible founders make this an attractive small, capital-light pilot worth modest prize funding and mentorship, but thin per-user economics, an inflated market sizing, untested trust/payment infrastructure, leakage risk and limited defensibility make it uncertain as a scalable venture. Moderate investment interest, better suited to a prize or pre-seed grant than a venture round at this stage.

Business plan text:

Hemline Swap
HEMLINE SWAP: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Problem
College students face a recurring expense that makes little economic sense. Galas, sorority and
fraternity formals, career fairs, interviews, cultural events and graduation all demand
formalwear, and most students own little of it. They buy outfits for a single night, wear them
once or twice, and then store them. In a survey we ran at our university with 412 respondents,
the average student spent 118 dollars on formalwear in the past year and wore each piece an
average of 1.4 times. Sixty-one percent said they had bought something for an event that they
never wore again. For students on tight budgets, 118 dollars is a meaningful sum, and for
first-generation and lower-income students the pressure to look the part at an interview or a
formal can be a real barrier to participation. Existing options do not solve this well.
Commercial rental services are priced for adults with salaries, ship by mail with fixed windows
and sizing risk, and rarely cover the specific styles students want. Resale apps are built for
everyday fashion, not for borrowing a dress for Saturday.
Solution
Hemline Swap is a mobile marketplace built specifically for one-night formalwear among college
students. A student photographs an item, tags the size, style, occasion and condition, and
lists it in under two minutes. Other students on the same campus browse by event type, size and
date, and request a rental, a swap or a purchase. Because users are on the same campus, pickup
and return happen in person within a day, which removes shipping delays and fit uncertainty,
since students can ask a classmate how an item runs. Payment, a refundable damage deposit and a
rating system are handled in the app. Listing is free, so supply grows from the closets
students already have. We think the product is distinctive because it combines three things
competitors do not: hyperlocal supply, event-based search, and a student-only trust layer using
verified university accounts.
Market
There are roughly 19 million students enrolled in US colleges and universities. If we assume
that a typical student attends three to four formal events a year and spends between 100 and
150 dollars annually on formalwear, annual campus formalwear spending is in the range of 2
billion to 3 billion dollars. We treat this as our addressable market. Our initial serviceable
market is the set of mid-size and large residential campuses with active Greek life, formals
and career programs, which we estimate at about 600 institutions and 6 million students. If
Hemline Swap captured just five percent of that serviceable spending through rentals priced
well below purchase, annual transaction volume would exceed 50 million dollars. Our pilot
suggests demand is concentrated around predictable seasonal peaks, such as formal season in
autumn and spring and the interview season, which helps us plan inventory and marketing.
Business Model
Hemline Swap earns revenue three ways. First, we take a 15 percent service fee on every rental,
charged to the borrower on top of the lender price. Second, we take a 10 percent fee on resales
completed in the app. Third, we sell optional protection, a 2 dollar per rental damage waiver
that reduces deposit friction. Typical rentals in the pilot were priced at 15 to 35 dollars,
against a purchase price of 80 to 200 dollars for the same item, so borrowers save roughly 70
percent and lenders earn money on items that would otherwise sit unused. Our pilot average
order was 31 dollars of transaction volume, which implies about 4.65 dollars of fee revenue per
rental before protection add-ons. We expect a returning user to rent 3 to 4 times a year, and
since customer acquisition on campus is largely organic through events, student organizations
and word of mouth, we expect acquisition costs to remain low. Later revenue options include
sponsored listings from local tailors and dry cleaners, and a cleaning-and-return service that
students can add for a fee.

Competition
The closest alternatives fall into three groups. Mail-order rental subscriptions offer large
catalogs but cost more per use, impose shipping windows, and are aimed at working adults.
General resale and peer-to-peer fashion apps have large audiences but optimize for permanent
ownership, not borrowing for a specific date, and offer no campus-level trust or fast pickup.
Informal channels, such as group chats and social media posts asking to borrow a dress, are
free and already common, which is evidence of demand, but they are unorganized, unreliable and
offer no protection if an item is damaged or never returned. Our advantage is that we serve the
exact moment students need an outfit, from people nearby whom they can verify, with payment and
protection built in. The main risk is that a larger platform adds a campus mode. We intend to
defend against this by building density on each campus first and by working with student
organizations, which creates relationships a general app will find hard to copy.
Team
Priya Raghunathan, chief executive, is a senior in business administration who ran the
formalwear closet for her sorority and observed the problem firsthand. She leads strategy,
partnerships and campus operations. Marcus Delacroix-Boyd, chief technology officer, is a
senior in computer science who built the first version of the app and previously completed two
summer internships in mobile development. Tamsin Okafor-Lindqvist, head of growth and design,
is a junior in marketing and design who led our user research and designed the brand and
listing experience. The team has complementary skills across operations, engineering and
growth, and has worked together for eight months.
Milestones and Financials
We have defined the core concept, registered the company, and launched a working version of the
app. In a six-week pilot on one campus, 187 students created accounts, 241 items were listed,
and 63 students completed paid rentals, generating 1,940 dollars in transaction volume and
about 291 dollars in fee revenue. Of renters, 44 percent completed a second rental within the
pilot window, and the average lender earned 37 dollars. Our costs to date are modest, covering
app store fees, hosting and printed materials, at roughly 2,400 dollars funded personally by
the founders. We have not yet formed a legal entity for the business and plan to do so with
legal support before taking any prize money. Our forecast for the next twelve months assumes
launch on four additional campuses, 3,500 registered users, 1,400 paid renters and about 55,000
dollars in transaction volume, producing roughly 9,000 dollars in fee revenue. We expect to
reach break-even on direct costs within a year and to fund growth from a mix of competition
prizes and a small seed round.
What We Ask For
We are asking for prize funding of 25,000 dollars, mentorship from experienced marketplace and
consumer app founders, and help with legal formation and trust and safety policy. The funds
would be allocated roughly as follows: 10,000 dollars for engineering time to add in-app
payments, damage protection and verified student onboarding; 9,000 dollars for launch marketing
and student ambassador programs on four campuses; 4,000 dollars for legal formation, insurance
and terms of service; and 2,000 dollars for operating costs. With this support we aim to prove
that the model repeats across campuses and to be ready for a seed round after the next formal
season.
Question: Share the strengths and weaknesses that you considered to arrive at your investment interest rating.
